title: CPC Calculator
description: Find the average cost of each advertising click.
example: A campaign spending 1,000 for 500 clicks has an average CPC of 2.
limitations: Enter spend and clicks from the same campaign, currency and reporting period. Average CPC does not predict an individual auction price.

title: CPM Calculator
description: Compare advertising costs per thousand impressions.
example: A spend of 1,000 and 200,000 impressions gives a CPM of 5.
limitations: Use served impressions rather than reach. Repeated displays count as separate impressions; viewable CPM may use a different denominator.

title: CTR Calculator
description: Measure the percentage of impressions that produce clicks.
example: 500 clicks from 20,000 impressions produces a 2.5% click-through rate.
limitations: Use consistent click and impression definitions. Repeated clicks can make this arithmetic ratio exceed 100%; compare like-for-like reporting metrics.

title: CPA Calculator
description: Work out your advertising cost for each conversion.
example: A spend of 1,000 for 50 acquisitions produces a CPA of 20.
limitations: Define the conversion event before comparing campaigns. This advertising metric excludes fulfillment costs and attribution outside your chosen reporting window.

title: Discount Calculator
description: Calculate sale price and savings from a percentage discount.
formula: Savings = original price × discount ÷ 100. Sale price = original price − savings.
example: An 80 item with a 25% discount saves 20 and has a sale price of 60.
limitations: Accepts discounts from 0% to 100%. Tax, shipping, currency rounding and stacked promotions are excluded.

title: Markup Calculator
description: See your markup on cost and profit per item.
formula: Markup (%) = (selling price − unit cost) ÷ unit cost × 100.
example: Buying an item for 60 and selling it for 100 produces 40 profit and 66.6667% markup.
limitations: Markup uses cost as the denominator; profit margin uses revenue. Include the costs relevant to your decision. Selling below cost produces a negative markup.

title: Break-even Calculator
description: Estimate the whole units needed to cover fixed costs.
formula: Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (selling price per unit − variable cost per unit), rounded upward.
example: Fixed costs of 1,000, a selling price of 25 and variable cost of 15 require 100 units to break even.
limitations: Assumes constant unit price and costs and that all units sell. A price at or below variable cost has no finite break-even point. Taxes and changes in capacity are excluded.

title: Bleed & Trim Calculator
description: Add bleed to final trim dimensions before print export.
formula: Artwork width = trim width + 2 × bleed per edge; the same formula applies to height.
example: A 210 × 297 mm trim with 3 mm bleed on every edge needs 216 × 303 mm artwork.
limitations: This calculates dimensions only and does not edit artwork or add crop marks. Ask your printer about bleed, safe zones and binding allowances.

title: Print Size Converter
description: Convert image and print dimensions between pixels, inches, centimeters and millimeters.
formula: Inches = millimeters ÷ 25.4. Pixels = inches × pixels per inch (PPI).
example: At 300 PPI, an image measuring 3,000 × 2,400 pixels converts to 10 × 8 inches or 254 × 203.2 mm.
limitations: PPI relates image pixels to physical size and is distinct from a printer’s ink-dot DPI. This converter does not resample an image. Pixel results show exact values and nearest whole pixels.

title: Video File Size & Bitrate Calculator
description: Estimate video file size or calculate a video bitrate budget.
formula: File bytes = duration in seconds × (video Mbps + audio kbps ÷ 1,000) × 1,000,000 ÷ 8. Target video Mbps = target MB × 8 ÷ seconds − audio Mbps.
example: A 60-second video at 8 Mbps plus 128 kbps audio is about 60.96 MB, or 58.136 MiB. A 60.96 MB target gives an 8 Mbps video budget.
limitations: Uses decimal MB and Mbps, with MiB also shown for size estimates. Assumes average bitrates; container overhead, variable-rate peaks and encoding quality affect real files. This tool does not encode or upload video.

title: Frames & Duration Converter
description: Convert frame counts to seconds and durations to whole frames.
formula: Duration in seconds = total frames ÷ frame rate. Frames = duration × frame rate, rounded to the nearest whole frame.
example: 300 frames at 30 frames per second last 10 seconds. At 29.97 fps, the same 300 frames last about 10.0100 seconds.
limitations: Uses a constant decimal frame rate and seconds, not drop-frame timecode. Enter the actual rate used by your project; 29.97 and 30 fps are different rates.
